title: Pauri 33, sound: aakhan jor
tomorrow: Pauri 33, meaning: no power of our own

segments.voice: Yesterday, Pauri 32 and the steps of the ladder. Your line was step by step. Did you take the first step of something you'd been dreading? Today, the next rung, sound first. Day two hundred eighteen.

Have you ever tried not to laugh? A quiet classroom, a serious meeting, a moment when laughing is the worst thing you could do. And it rises anyway. You bite your cheek, you stare at the floor, and your shoulders shake. Or the opposite: you want to say the right thing to a grieving friend, and nothing comes out at all. We think of speaking and staying quiet as the two things we control best. Open mouth, close mouth. Pauri 33 opens with exactly those two, and one hard little word that keeps coming back like a hammer. Today, just listen to it.
screen: `TRYING NOT TO LAUGH.` → `THE WORDS THAT WON'T COME.` → `ONE WORD, LIKE A HAMMER.`

segments.voice: Here is the first line of Pauri 33: aakhan jor, chupai nah jor. Four sounds to learn. Aakhan: speaking, saying. It's the same root as aakheeah in yesterday's stanza, where the Name was said on a million tongues. Jor: power, force, strength. It's a Persian word that's still alive in Punjabi and Hindi; people say it when they mean push hard, put your strength into it. Chupai: in silence. You may know chup from Punjabi, as in chup kar, be quiet. Nah: not, no. So: no power to speak, no power to keep silent. Commentators read that nah across both halves of the line. Now listen to its shape. Jor lands at the end of each half: aakhan jor, chupai nah jor. Two short beats, then the heavy one. And the next line flips it around, so jor comes first and last: jor na mangan, den na jor. No power to ask, no power to give. The word boxes the line in. The whole stanza keeps doing this. Jor, jor, jor, a dozen times or more, each time with na or nah beside it, like someone knocking on door after door and finding every one locked. Tomorrow we'll open which doors, and whose hand holds the key. Today, feel the hammer. It's a stanza you can almost recite by the rhythm alone, and many people who love the Japji say this is the one they learned first by ear.
screen: `AAKHAN — SPEAKING.` · `JOR — POWER, FORCE.` · `CHUPAI NAH JOR — NOR TO BE SILENT.` · `JOR, AGAIN AND AGAIN, LIKE A HAMMER.` · then, large: `AAKHAN JOR.`

segments.voice: Say the first line aloud, slowly: aakhan jor, chupai nah jor. Say it three times, and let jor land heavy each time, like a hand on a table. Then try the next line too: jor na mangan, den na jor. After that, stop speaking, and simply stay silent. Notice that even the silence isn't quite yours: thoughts keep talking. Don't fight them. Let them knock and pass. The bell holds the time.
Pauri 33. It opens: aakhan jor, chupai nah jor, no power to speak, no power to be silent, and the word jor keeps coming back like a hammer.
Your line: aakhan jor. Today, notice one moment when words came out that you didn't plan, or didn't come when you wanted them. Just notice. Day two hundred eighteen.

howItsDone: Many Sikhs recite Japji Sahib each morning; Pauri 33's repeated word jor, power, gives it a strong rhythm that many learn by ear, often before they know what each line means.

original.note: Gurmukhi, Japji Pauri 33: no power to speak, no power to keep silent.

trapdoor: what you thought: a line about talking.
what it means: even speaking and staying quiet are not fully in our power.
what a scholar hears: jor is Persian zor, force; the negative is read across both halves, and later lines box themselves in with jor at start and end.
